title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Policy Training** (Vol IV). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

A learned policy acquires its behavior from the experience its training supplies, and its weights keep no record of which experience that was. Demonstrations can omit the recovery from a displaced fixture, a simulator can reward a fast approach that a real contact surface cannot tolerate, and a model pretrained on other robots can behave plausibly in conditions no one has tested on this machine.

nodes.label: Dual Failure Modes of Policy Training
The Simulator as a System Component
Physical Channels of the Sim-to-Real Gap

rows: **Training-regime hidden dependency**

A policy's weights keep what its experience rewarded but not which experience it was, so each regime (demonstrations, logged rewards, simulation, trial on the machine, a pretrained base) leaves a characteristic dependency no training score shows.
**Mode averaging**

The squared-error optimum of a point-regression policy is the conditional mean of the action, so two valid evasions average to an action no demonstrator chose, and more data or capacity cannot fix it.
**Decoder renewal slack**

A decoder chosen for multimodality must fit the proposal deadline, since latency is encoding plus every dependent decoder evaluation, so the head and evaluation count that training picks decide schedulability.
**Offline RL support limit**
Fitting values over a fixed log and acting greedily inflates values at actions the log never executed, and conservative objectives reduce that error but cannot create support the log lacks.
**Physical RL exploration cost**
A trial campaign's wall clock is trials times rollout plus reset over rigs (about 93 days of execution for 10^6 latch trials before resets), and every trial spends heat and drivetrain life.
**Reality gap as a vector**
Sim-to-real mismatch decomposes into dynamics, sensing, appearance, and timing channels, each sized by paired probing, and randomization covers modeled parameters but never omitted mechanisms.
**Update is a new checkpoint**
On-machine fine-tuning absorbs a measurable local mismatch but produces new weights whose earlier evaluations no longer apply, and a gated residual bounds where adaptation may act.
**Policy manifest**

The policy manifest records how a checkpoint was produced (regime sequence, base digest, inference contract, data support, omission log, wear log) and computes the declared ODD as support minus omissions.
**Reward as specification**
Posing the task as an MDP makes the engineer-written reward and discount the whole objective, so the optimizer exploits any omitted or mismeasured term.
**Pretrained borrowed competence**
Post-training a pretrained generalist can cut task-data needs, but no pretraining episode joins this machine's scenario table, so it supplies competence, not evidence.
**Simulator contact exploit**
A simulator's contact model decides what the optimizer learns, and a soft penalty spring lets a policy pass through contacts the real plate would resist.
**Privileged information limits**
Asymmetric critics and teacher-student distillation speed training under partial observability, but the student cannot recover a state its sensors never observe.
**Paired probing**
Identical open-loop excitations on the robot and its simulated twin, scored against error budgets per channel, size each component of the reality gap.
**Velocity versus torque drift**
A velocity-commanded policy has a disturbance-rejecting loop beneath it and its error integrates once, while a torque-commanded policy's error integrates twice.
**Chunk imitation objective**
Chunked imitation fits a horizon of actions with a Huber penalty on normalized residuals, which buys outlier robustness, not smoothness or feasibility.
**RL value functions**
State value, action value, advantage, and the Bellman relation express value as negated cost-to-go, with LQR as the closed-form linear-quadratic case.
